tldr: This is a topic cluster, not one event: early-November papers proposed a runtime defense for tool-using agents and widened injection testing to task tampering and injected reasoning. A Nov 8 paper argued for treating the model as untrusted, and practitioner posts followed with a lawyerspeak guardrail bypass and a case for authorization scoping.
whats_new: A Nov 23 paper, Conartist, reports adaptive multi-step injection succeeding 32.12% of the time on a 576-instance tool-use benchmark and 66.67% on a Reddit GUI benchmark across five backbone models.
why_it_matters: Adaptive, multi-step attacks against computer-using agents land often enough that a text-reading guardrail cannot be the last line; the control that holds is the permission boundary enforced in code around each tool call.

beats.headline: SPILLWAY separates target admission from sanitization
beats.summary: Argues against putting an LLM on the decision that lets an action through, since that decision can itself be manipulated.

beats.headline: Benchmarks add task tampering and thought injection
beats.summary: Attacks move past instruction override: attacker content can alter the outcome of the user's own task, or target a reasoning model's chain-of-thought stage.

beats.headline: Paper frames injection as structural and treats the model as untrusted
beats.summary: Compares in-prompt defences (hardened prompts, spotlighting) against deterministic policy enforcement, human approval, and taint tracking, validated on open-weights models.

beats.headline: Practitioner post claims guardrail bypass using lawyerspeak
beats.summary: A write-up on defeating agent guardrails with legal-style language, the first non-paper item in the thread.

beats.headline: Practitioner guidance: scope agent authorization to limit injection damage
beats.summary: Stack Builders frames authorization, not detection, as the control that caps what an injected agent can do.

beats.headline: Conartist automates adaptive multi-step injection against computer-using agents
beats.summary: A two-stage adaptive red-teaming framework reports 32.12% attack success on tool use and 66.67% on a Reddit GUI benchmark.

beats.headline: FATCAT: hardware fault injection bypasses on-device alignment
beats.summary: Not prompt injection: an electromagnetic fault-injection attack on GPU SoCs makes Llama 3.2 1B and Gemma 3 1B fulfill refused requests, clustered here by shared vocabulary.

open_questions: Does SPILLWAY's admission/sanitization split keep its robustness in independent evaluation on real agent frameworks?
Which guardrail products does the lawyerspeak bypass work against, and do their vendors confirm or patch it?
Do deterministic policy enforcement and taint tracking hold on closed frontier models, beyond the open-weights models the paper validated on?
How far does Conartist's attack success rate fall against agents that run under deterministic policy enforcement or scoped credentials?
Do agent frameworks ship per-tool, per-task scoped credentials by default, or is authorization scoping still left to each team?
take_for_builders: Give each agent task the narrowest credentials it needs and gate high-impact tool calls with deterministic policy or human approval, then add adaptive multi-step, task-tampering, and legal-register cases to your red-team suite.
